Alice.summary: The proposition expressed by a sentence is the set of possible worlds in which that sentence is true.

Bob.summary: A proposition is an ordered tuple composed of the referents of the sentence's sub-expressions.

c1.text: The proposition expressed by a sentence is the set of possible worlds in which that sentence is true.

c2.text: A proposition is an ordered tuple composed of the referents of the sentence's sub-expressions.

c3.text: The proposition expressed by 'Suchul loves Heeyoung' is <a, b, r>, where a is Suchul, b is Heeyoung, and r is the binary relation 'loves'.

c4.text: If a sentence is true in every possible world, the proposition it expresses is the set of all possible worlds.

c5.text: Sentences express different propositions if the sets of possible worlds in which they are true are different sets.

ha1.text: 'Suchul loves Heeyoung' and 'Heeyoung loves Suchul' express different propositions.

ha3.text: When Suchul and Heeyoung are different objects, the set of possible worlds where Suchul loves Heeyoung is different from the set of possible worlds where Heeyoung loves Suchul.

ha4.text: The proposition expressed by 'Heeyoung loves Suchul' is <b, a, r>, where b is Heeyoung, a is Suchul, and r is 'loves'.

ha5.text: Since a and b are different objects, <a, b, r> and <b, a, r> are different ordered triplets.

a.note: Both Alice and Bob derive that the two sentences express different propositions when Suchul and Heeyoung refer to different objects.

hb1.text: The sentences 'A round square exists' and '3 is odd and not odd' have different meanings.

hb2.text: 'A round square exists' and '3 is odd and not odd' are both false in every possible world, so their sets of possible worlds are both the empty set.

hb3.text: The proposition expressed by a sentence is not the set of possible worlds in which that sentence is true.

b.note: Believing two impossible sentences with identical truth sets (empty set) have different meanings attacks Alice's thesis that propositions are truth sets across possible worlds.

hc1.text: 'Morning Star' and 'Evening Star' refer to the same object.

hc2.text: The sentences 'The Morning Star is beautiful' and 'The Evening Star is beautiful' have different meanings.

hc3.text: A proposition is not an ordered tuple composed of the referents of the sentence's sub-expressions.

c.note: When two names co-refer, believing sentences differing only by those names have different meanings attacks Bob's thesis that propositions are ordered tuples of referents.
